text: What are the three key strategies for minimising disruption when troubleshooting?

options.text: Reboot, Replace, Report
Replacements, Backups, Systematic Approach
Diagnose, Fix, Document
Linear, Half-Split, Documentation

explanation: The three key strategies for minimising disruption are: Replacements, Backups, and using a Systematic Approach.

text: What is the replacement strategy in troubleshooting?

options.text: Spend as long as needed diagnosing the faulty component before touching anything
Swap out the faulty component for a known working replacement to restore the system quickly, then investigate the fault separately
Replace the entire system rather than individual components
Order a replacement part and wait until it arrives before starting work

explanation: The replacement strategy means swapping the faulty component for a known working one to get the system back up quickly. The faulty part is then investigated separately without causing further downtime.

text: What is the key principle behind using replacements to minimise disruption?

options.text: Investigate first, restore later
Restore first, investigate later
Replace everything and see what works
Only replace if the fault cannot be diagnosed

explanation: The principle is 'Restore first, investigate later' — get the user or system back up and running quickly, then diagnose the faulty component separately.

text: Why are backups important before starting troubleshooting work?

options.text: They speed up the diagnostic process
If something goes wrong during troubleshooting — such as data loss — you can restore to a working state quickly
They are required by law before any technical work
They allow you to skip the documentation step

explanation: Having up-to-date backups means that if something goes wrong during troubleshooting — such as data loss or system instability — you can restore to a working state quickly.

text: What should you always confirm before starting work on a system?

options.text: That the user has logged out
That a backup exists
That the fault has been reproduced three times
That all cables are unplugged

explanation: The key principle for backups is 'Verify before you start' — never begin work on a system without confirming a backup exists.

text: What is the systematic approach to minimising disruption?

options.text: Try random fixes quickly until something works
Follow a structured, methodical process such as the 8-step model and record everything
Fix the most obvious problem first without planning
Ask the user to describe the fault, then immediately replace the most likely component

explanation: The systematic approach means following a structured process like the 8-step model. Random guesswork without recording what you've done is one of the most common causes of extended downtime.

text: What is one of the most common causes of extended downtime during troubleshooting?

options.text: Using the Half-Split approach on a simple system
Random guesswork without recording what has been done
Having too many replacement parts available
Starting work before the user has reported the fault

explanation: Random guesswork without recording what you have done is one of the most common causes of extended downtime and can create new problems.

text: What is the key principle that applies across ALL three disruption minimisation strategies?

options.text: Fix quickly regardless of process
Plan before you act
Always replace rather than repair
Document only at the end

explanation: The key principle across all three strategies is 'Plan before you act'. Rushing in without preparation tends to make things worse, not better.

text: What can happen if you rush into troubleshooting without preparation?

options.text: The fault is usually found faster
Things tend to get worse, not better
The backup is automatically triggered
The systematic approach kicks in automatically

explanation: Rushing in without preparation tends to make things worse, not better. Planning before acting is essential across all three disruption minimisation strategies.

text: A server has crashed and users cannot work. What is the best first step to minimise disruption?

options.text: Spend several hours fully diagnosing the root cause before making any changes
Swap in a known working replacement to restore service, then investigate the faulty component separately
Delete all recent changes to return the system to its original state
Wait for the manufacturer to provide a fix

explanation: The replacement strategy says restore first, investigate later. Swapping in a working replacement gets users back up quickly while the fault is diagnosed separately without further downtime.

text: A technician is about to apply a software patch to fix a fault. What should they verify first?

options.text: That the patch was released within the last 30 days
That a backup exists before starting work
That all users are logged off the system
That the fault has been reported in writing

explanation: The key backup principle is 'Verify before you start'. Never begin work on a system without confirming a backup exists — the patch could cause data loss or instability.

text: Which badge summarises the systematic approach strategy?

options.text: Restore first, investigate later
Verify before you start
Plan before you act
Test before you deploy

explanation: 'Plan before you act' is the principle for the systematic approach. 'Restore first, investigate later' applies to replacements, and 'Verify before you start' applies to backups.
